blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 30 (Spectroscopy-2 NMR), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is NMR spectroscopy? Give its uses and name its two common methods. Explain why only some nuclei give NMR signals. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a powerful technique based on the magnetic properties (nuclear spin) of nuclei.

Uses: chemistry, the polymer industry, the study of proteins and natural products, environment monitoring and the medical field. In chemistry it is used particularly to identify organic compounds and determine their structures.

Two common methods: proton (¹H) NMR and carbon-13 (¹³C) NMR.

Which nuclei give signals: atoms with odd mass numbers, e.g. ¹H and ¹³C, usually show signals; their nuclei behave like tiny magnets. Nuclei with even atomic and even mass numbers, e.g. ¹²C, have an even number of protons and of neutrons (not always equal; ¹⁸O has 8 protons and 10 neutrons). The protons pair their spins and the neutrons pair theirs, so there is no net magnetic field and no NMR signal.

book_ref.quote: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a powerful technique

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the principle of proton (¹H) NMR spectroscopy. Use methanol to explain how NMR identifies hydrogen atoms in different environments. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nuclear spin: nuclei such as ¹H behave like tiny magnets.

1. No magnetic field: all the nuclei have random orientation and the same energy.
2. Strong magnetic field: the nuclei align either with or against the field, giving two spin states, a low energy state and a high energy state (Figure 30.1).
3. Spin flipping: on irradiation with radio waves, nuclei in the low energy state absorb energy and move to the high energy state.
4. Spectrum: when they return to their original states they emit energy, which is detected and converted into an NMR spectrum.

Molecular environment: the exact energy needed to flip a nucleus depends on its position in the compound and the surrounding atoms (the molecular environment). So hydrogens in different environments in one molecule absorb different energies.

Methanol, CH₃OH: three hydrogens are on carbon and one on oxygen. The -CH₃ and O-H hydrogens lie in different environments, so they absorb different frequencies of radio waves for flipping and appear as different signals.

Nuclei in different environments can also be flipped by radio waves of the same frequency if the magnetic field strength is varied.

book_ref.quote: When placed in a strong magnetic field, these nuclei align themselves

blocks.prompt: 3 Explain the problem caused by ordinary solvents in ¹H NMR and how deuterated solvents solve it. Why is TMS added as well? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Problem: the sample is dissolved in excess solvent. Ordinary solvents contain hydrogen atoms which produce strong signals and interfere with the spectrum. If CHCl₃ were used, the signal of its single proton would be intense enough to overlap completely and mask the weaker signals of the sample's protons.

Solution: deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃ (deuterated chloroform) or CD₃OD (deuterated methanol) are used. In CDCl₃ hydrogen is replaced by its isotope deuterium (D). Deuterium needs a different frequency of radio waves for flipping, so it does not absorb the radio frequency given to the sample and its peak does not appear in the ¹H spectrum. The solvent is 'silent' and only the sample's signals are seen.

TMS: tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄, is the standard reference. Its signal is set at 0.0 ppm and every other signal is measured from it. Its 12 equivalent protons give one sharp peak at the extreme right (low electronegativity of silicon), away from most organic signals; it is inert and volatile, so it is easily removed.

book_ref.quote: In the ¹H NMR analysis the sample to be analyzed is dissolved in excess solvent

blocks.prompt: 4 Define chemical shift. Explain how the electron density around a proton affects its chemical shift, using the spectrum of methanol. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chemical shift (δ): the position of a peak in a ¹H NMR spectrum relative to the TMS peak; it is measured in parts per million (ppm). TMS is assigned 0.0 ppm. A ¹H spectrum has a δ range of 0 – 12 ppm.

Chemical shift indicates the electronic environment of a proton: protons in different environments have different δ values, those in the same environment have the same δ value.

Effect of electron density: protons are surrounded by electrons, and this electron density affects the spectrum.
• Protons surrounded by high electron density (alkyl groups) have lower δ values.
• Protons with low electron density, near electronegative atoms like F, O, N, Cl, appear at higher δ values.

Methanol (Figure 30.2): the -CH₃ protons have higher electron density around them and appear at 3.35 ppm. The O-H proton is next to electronegative oxygen and appears at 4.80 ppm. The difference of each peak from the TMS peak (0.0 ppm) is its chemical shift.

book_ref.quote: Chemical shift is an important parameter in NMR spectroscopy

blocks.prompt: 5 What are chemically equivalent protons? Explain with examples of molecules having one, two and three proton environments. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Protons in different parts of a molecule are in different environments because of the atoms and bonds near them.

Chemically equivalent protons: all the protons found in chemically identical environments within a molecule. They show the same chemical shift.

One environment: all the protons of TMS, methane, ethane, benzene and propanone (acetone) are equivalent, so each gives a single absorption peak (Figure 30.3, methane).

Two environments: methanol, CH₃OH. The three -CH₃ protons are one set and the O-H proton is another; two peaks (3.35 and 4.80 ppm).

Three environments: ethanol, C₂H₅OH. A proton on -CH₃ differs from one on -CH₂- and from the O-H proton. All three -CH₃ protons share one environment and the two -CH₂- protons share another, so there are three sets and three peaks.

A molecule with sets of chemically different protons has different chemical shifts and gives more than one peak.

book_ref.quote: Protons in different parts of a molecule are in different "environments"

blocks.prompt: 6 What information does a low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum give? Interpret the low-resolution spectrum of ethanol (Figure 30.4). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A low-resolution spectrum gives three main pieces of information: the number of different proton environments, the types of these environments and the relative number of protons in each. Three parameters are analysed:

1. Number of peaks: corresponds to the number of different chemical environments of protons.
2. Chemical shift of each peak: corresponds to the type of environment (compare with Table 30.1).
3. Area under each peak: proportional to the number of protons giving that peak.

Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (Figure 30.4):
• Three peaks, so three proton environments: CH₃, CH₂ and OH.
• 5.4 ppm: OH (low electron density); 3.7 ppm: –CH₂– next to oxygen; 1.2 ppm: –CH₃.
• Peaks labelled 1H, 2H and 3H: relative areas 1 : 2 : 3, matching OH (1), CH₂ (2) and CH₃ (3).
• Total hydrogens = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

book_ref.quote: A low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum provides three main pieces of information

blocks.prompt: 7 A compound C₈H₁₀ gives three ¹H NMR peaks at 7.2, 2.6 and 1.2 ppm with relative areas 16.0 : 6.4 : 9.6. Find the number of protons in each environment and identify each type of proton using Table 30.1. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Peak area is proportional to the number of protons: reduce the areas to a whole-number ratio, check against the formula, then read the type from the δ ranges.

book_ref.quote: The intensity ratio shows that they are present in the ratio of 1:2:3

steps: Multiply by 2 for whole numbers: 5 : 2 : 3
Sum = 5 + 2 + 3 = 10, equal to the 10 H in C₈H₁₀, so the peaks have 5 H, 2 H and 3 H
7.2 ppm (5 H): in 6.5 – 9.0 ppm, aromatic protons Ar–H
2.6 ppm (2 H): in 2.3 – 3.0 ppm, –CH₂– next to an aromatic ring
1.2 ppm (3 H): in 0.5 – 1.5 ppm, alkyl –CH₃
blocks.final_answer: 5 H (Ar–H, 7.2 ppm), 2 H (–CH₂–Ar, 2.6 ppm) and 3 H (–CH₃, 1.2 ppm): the compound is C₆H₅–CH₂–CH₃ (ethylbenzene).

blocks.prompt: 8 What is meant by splitting of signals in high-resolution ¹H NMR? State the n+1 rule and explain the high-resolution spectrum of ethanol. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
NMR signals are affected not only by nearby electrons but also by protons on adjacent atoms. In a high-resolution spectrum each peak is often a cluster of sub-peaks, because each signal is split by the protons on the adjacent carbon atoms.

Splitting of signals: the splitting into multiple peaks (doublets, triplets, quartets) indicates the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atom.

n+1 rule: a signal usually splits into n + 1 sub-peaks, where n is the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atom(s).
Number of sub-peaks = n + 1

Ethanol, CH₃–CH₂–OH (Figure 30.5):
• -CH₃: the adjacent carbon has 2 protons, 2 + 1 = 3 sub-peaks: triplet.
• -CH₂-: the adjacent carbon has 3 protons, 3 + 1 = 4 sub-peaks: quartet.
• -OH: not split, because its hydrogen is bonded to oxygen instead of carbon: singlet.

book_ref.quote: When a high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of a molecule is studied

blocks.prompt: 9 Which protons do not show or cause splitting? Explain with ethane. Give the common splitting patterns of Table 30.2. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
No splitting cases:
1. -OH and -NH protons usually do not show splitting; they appear as a singlet.
2. Chemically equivalent protons do not cause splitting of their neighbouring protons.

Ethane, CH₃–CH₃: if one methyl group is considered, its adjacent carbon has 3 protons, so a quartet might be expected. But all six hydrogens of ethane are chemically equivalent, so the peak is not split; ethane gives a single singlet (Figure 30.6).

Common splitting patterns (Table 30.2):

book_ref.quote: Similarly, chemically equivalent protons do not cause splitting of their neighbouring protons

blocks.prompt: 10 Use the n+1 rule to find the number of sub-peaks and the splitting pattern of every signal of methyl propanoate, CH₃–CH₂–CO–O–CH₃. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: For each set of equivalent protons count n, the protons on the adjacent carbon atom(s); then sub-peaks = n + 1. Atoms without hydrogen (C=O carbon, O) add nothing to n.

book_ref.quote: Number of sub-peaks can be calculated by using 'n+1' rule

steps: Environments: CH₃ (of the ethyl part), CH₂ (next to C=O) and O–CH₃: three signals
CH₃ of the ethyl part: adjacent CH₂ has 2 H, n = 2, sub-peaks = 2 + 1 = 3: triplet
CH₂: adjacent CH₃ has 3 H and the C=O carbon has none, n = 3, sub-peaks = 3 + 1 = 4: quartet
O–CH₃: its neighbour is O (no H), n = 0, sub-peaks = 0 + 1 = 1: singlet
Integration: 3 : 2 : 3 (total 8 H, C₄H₈O₂)
blocks.final_answer: CH₃ triplet (3 sub-peaks), CH₂ quartet (4 sub-peaks), O–CH₃ singlet (1 sub-peak); areas 3 : 2 : 3.

blocks.prompt: 11 A compound shows two singlets and it is not clear which is due to an O-H proton. Explain why such a proton is hard to identify, and how deuterium exchange settles it. Give the equations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Why it is hard: the hydrogens in O-H (alcohols, carboxylic acids) and N-H (amines, amides) are easily exchangeable, so their singlet shows a wide range of δ and is difficult to identify. Exchange of ethanol with water:
CH₃–CH₂–O–Hᵃ + Hᵇ–O–Hᵇ ⇌ CH₃–CH₂–O–Hᵇ + Hᵃ–O–Hᵇ

Deuterium exchange (D₂O shake):
1. Record the ¹H spectrum; it shows all the H atoms including O–H.
2. Add a few drops of D₂O to the sample tube, shake well and record the spectrum again.
3. Compare: the singlet that has disappeared in the second spectrum belonged to the O–H proton; the singlet that remains is due to C–H protons.

Reason: protons attached to highly electronegative atoms like O or N are quickly exchanged with deuterium:
R–O–H + D₂O ⇌ R–O–D + HOD
Deuterium requires a different energy for spin flipping than ¹H, so it shows no peak in the ¹H spectrum; it is 'invisible'.

book_ref.quote: Sometimes, it becomes very difficult to identify these peaks in spectra

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe the steps for predicting the ¹H NMR spectrum of a molecule. Apply them to ethanal, CH₃CHO. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Steps:
I. Identify the different proton environments; number of environments = number of peaks expected.
II. Estimate δ for each set from Table 30.1; without the table, check the nearest bonds and atoms (near electronegative elements: higher δ; alkyl: lower δ).
III. Predict the splitting of each peak by the n+1 rule.
IV. Assign integration ratios according to the number of H atoms in each environment.

Ethanal, CH₃–CHO:

book_ref.quote: After understanding the concepts of chemical environment, chemical shift and splitting of peaks

rows: one set (1 H); 2 peaks in all

blocks.prompt: 13 Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of bromoethane, CH₃–CH₂–Br, and of methoxymethane, CH₃–O–CH₃. Explain why the two spectra differ. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bromoethane, CH₃–CH₂–Br (worked like Example 30.1):
• Peaks: two environments (CH₃ and CH₂), so 2 peaks.
• δ: CH₂ is attached to an electronegative halogen, so higher δ (3.0 – 4.5 ppm); CH₃ lower (0.5 – 1.5 ppm).
• Splitting: CH₃ has 2 neighbouring H, 2 + 1 = 3: triplet; CH₂ has 3 neighbouring H, 3 + 1 = 4: quartet.
• Area: CH₃ : CH₂ = 3 : 2.

Methoxymethane, CH₃–O–CH₃:
• Peaks: both CH₃ groups are in the same environment, so all six protons are equivalent: 1 peak.
• δ: CH₃–O, 3.0 – 4.5 ppm.
• Splitting: the neighbour is O with no H, n = 0: singlet.
• Area: one peak of 6 H.

Difference: bromoethane has two different, neighbouring proton sets that split each other; methoxymethane has only one set of equivalent protons with no protons on the adjacent atom.

book_ref.quote: Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane (CH₃-CH₂-Cl).

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe how the structure of an unknown compound is deduced from its ¹H NMR spectrum. Explain the working of Example 30.2 (the ester). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Steps (put the information together like a puzzle):
1. Count the peaks: number of proton environments (sets of equivalent protons), not the number of protons.
2. Use each chemical shift with the data table to identify functional groups.
3. Use the peak areas to find the number of H atoms in each environment.
4. Analyse the splitting: n = number of sub-peaks – 1 gives the adjacent protons.
5. Combine the information to assemble the structure.

Example 30.2 (ester):

book_ref.quote: The structure of an unknown compound can also be deduced by analyzing its ¹H NMR spectrum

rows: CH₂ next to electronegative O; n = 4 – 1 = 3 (CH₃–CH₂–O)

blocks.prompt: 15 A compound C₂H₄O gives two ¹H NMR peaks: a doublet at 2.2 ppm and a quartet at 9.8 ppm, with relative areas 7.5 : 2.5. Deduce its structure, showing each step. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use peaks, areas, shifts and splitting in turn, then join the pieces so that they fit C₂H₄O.

book_ref.quote: Count the number of peaks in the spectrum.

steps: Number of peaks = 2, so two proton environments
Areas: 7.5/2.5 : 2.5/2.5 = 3 : 1; sum 4 = the 4 H of C₂H₄O, so 3 H and 1 H
2.2 ppm (3 H): in 2.0 – 2.6 ppm, CH₃ next to C=O
9.8 ppm (1 H): in 9.0 – 10.0 ppm, aldehyde proton –CHO
Splitting: CH₃ doublet, n = 2 – 1 = 1 (next to the CHO hydrogen); CHO quartet, n = 4 – 1 = 3 (next to CH₃)
Combine: CH₃–CHO (C₂H₄O)

blocks.prompt: 16 A compound C₂H₄O₂ gives two singlets: 2.1 ppm and 11.4 ppm with relative areas 13.5 : 4.5. After a D₂O shake the 11.4 ppm peak disappears. Deduce the structure. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Reduce the areas to find H in each peak, read the groups from the shifts, use the singlets (no neighbours) and the D₂O result (O–H) to join them.

book_ref.quote: Use peak area to find the actual number of hydrogen atoms for each peak

steps: Two peaks: two proton environments
Areas: 13.5/4.5 : 4.5/4.5 = 3 : 1; sum 4 = the 4 H of C₂H₄O₂, so 3 H and 1 H
2.1 ppm (3 H): in 2.0 – 2.6 ppm, CH₃ next to C=O; singlet, n = 0
11.4 ppm (1 H): in 9.0 – 13.0 ppm, carboxylic acid; disappears on D₂O shake, so it is an O–H proton
Combine: CH₃–COOH (C₂H₄O₂)
blocks.final_answer: The compound is ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH.

blocks.prompt: 17 Explain the basis of ¹³C NMR spectroscopy. Compare ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR spectra. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Basis: the ¹²C nucleus has no magnetic property because of its even numbers of protons and neutrons (even mass number), so it is NMR inactive. The ¹³C nucleus possesses magnetic spin due to its odd number of neutrons, so ¹³C NMR spectra can be recorded for carbon compounds.

As in ¹H NMR, chemical shifts are measured relative to TMS (δ = 0.0 ppm), but the ¹³C range is 0 – 220 ppm. CDCl₃ is usually the solvent; it gives a small signal near 80 ppm.

Comparison:

book_ref.quote: On the basis of the magnetic properties of carbon-13 isotope

rows: Each peak = one carbon environment; simpler spectrum
Peak area shows the number of protons
Peak area usually not proportional to the number of carbons
Peaks not split; appear as vertical lines

blocks.prompt: 18 Explain the chemical environment of carbon atoms with examples. Give the chemical shift ranges of the main carbon environments from Table 30.3. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A carbon atom's environment is determined by the types of atoms directly attached to it. Carbons in the same environment are chemically equivalent and show the same chemical shift; carbons in different environments are non-equivalent and appear at different positions.

Examples: both carbons of ethane have the same environment. In 2-methylpropane the three methyl carbons have the same environment, while the tertiary carbon has a different one (two environments).

Table 30.3:

book_ref.quote: The type of environment can be predicted by looking at atoms or bonds around carbon atoms

blocks.prompt: 19 How is a ¹³C NMR spectrum predicted? Predict and explain the ¹³C spectra of ethane, propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, and interpret the spectrum of ethanol. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Each ¹³C peak corresponds to one different carbon environment, and its chemical shift tells about that environment:
Number of peaks = number of different carbon environments

• Ethane, CH₃–CH₃: both carbons in the same environment: 1 peak.
• Propan-1-ol, CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH: all three carbons differ: 3 peaks; only the CH₂ bonded to O lies in the C–O range 50 – 70 ppm.
• Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CH–OH: the two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, the CH–OH carbon differs: 2 peaks; the CH–O carbon at 50 – 70 ppm.

Ethanol, CH₃–CH₂–OH (Figure 30.7): two environments, two peaks. Using Table 30.3, the peak at 18 ppm is the -CH₃ carbon and the peak near 57 ppm is the -CH₂- carbon bonded to oxygen.

The peaks are not split (vertical lines) and their areas are usually not proportional to the number of carbons.

book_ref.quote: Similarly, two peaks are observed in the ¹³C spectrum of ethanol

blocks.prompt: 20 Describe the steps used to determine a structure from a ¹³C NMR spectrum. A compound C₃H₈O shows 3 peaks, only one of which is in the range 50 – 70 ppm. Decide between propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and methoxyethane (CH₃–O–CH₂–CH₃). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Steps:
1. Count the peaks: the number of different carbon environments. (Fewer peaks than carbons means some carbons are chemically equivalent.)
2. Look at the position (δ) of each peak and assign it with Table 30.3 (alkyl, next to O, alkene/aromatic, carbonyl ...).
3. Draw the possible structures that fit the molecular formula, work out the spectrum each would give, and keep the one that fits.

Application to C₃H₈O:
• Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CH–OH: 2 environments, 2 peaks; rejected by the count.
• Methoxyethane, CH₃–O–CH₂–CH₃: 3 environments, but two carbons (CH₃–O and O–CH₂) are bonded to oxygen, giving two peaks in 50 – 70 ppm; rejected by the positions.
• Propan-1-ol, CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH: 3 environments and only one carbon bonded to O, so one peak in 50 – 70 ppm and two in the alkyl range: fits.

The compound is propan-1-ol. As the book's own Figure 30.8 example shows, the peak count alone may fit more than one isomer; the shifts must be checked too.

book_ref.quote: The steps during the analysis of a spectrum are:
